# Suspense Versus Surprise

Surprise is what the reader feels when something they did not expect happens: a short jolt. Suspense is what they feel when they know, or fear, that something will happen and wait for it: a long pull. The familiar illustration is the bomb under the table. Shown to the audience, it makes a dull conversation unbearable; hidden, it gives fifteen seconds of shock.

## Why it matters for The Salt Choir

The whole structural argument of 2026 is about this distinction.

- **Draft 1** had neither. The storm was not hidden, the book's title points at a memorial, but nothing made the reader wait for it.
- **Draft 2** opened on the storm, which I thought created suspense about who would die. It did for a few chapters. Then, because the storm returned in fragments, readers worked out the crew, and the suspense became a countdown with the answer printed. [[marcus-ellery]] said it first: once readers know who dies, every chapter must make them want to know how ([[writing-group-2026-04-08]]).
- **Draft 3** keeps a short [[storm-prologue]] to create the long pull, and withholds names and outcome to keep the answer back.

## The live disagreement

[[callum-pryce]] says even a nameless prologue is the bomb shown too clearly: readers know the boat is lost. I say they know a boat goes out in a storm, and the question "who will not come back?" is the suspense. See [[should-the-salt-choir-keep-the-storm-prologue]] and [[a-prologue-must-earn-its-pages]].
